title: Proper semisimple Lie centralizers span the ambient tangent space
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field]. All groups are affine $k$-group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Smoothness and geometric connectedness have the meanings of [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme]. Fix an algebraic closure $\bar k$ [def-weil-algebraic-closure], and let $G$ be smooth and geometrically connected. For a smooth group $J$ put $\mathfrak j=\operatorname{Lie}(J)=T_{J/k,e}$ [def-sc-scheme-tangent-space], with its commutator Lie bracket [def-wf-lie-algebra]. Fix a faithful closed linear representation $i:G\hookrightarrow\operatorname{GL}_{n,k}$ [def-sc-general-linear-group, def-weil-closed-immersion]. Call $X\in\mathfrak g$ semisimple if $di(X)$ is diagonalizable over $\bar k$, and noncentral if $[X,Y]\ne0$ for some $Y\in\mathfrak g$. Assume $k$ is infinite and $\operatorname{Lie}(G_{\bar k})$ contains a noncentral semisimple element, using the base-changed representation. For each noncentral semisimple $X\in\mathfrak g$, let $K_X=C_G(X)^\circ$, where $C_G(X)(R)=\{g\in G(R):\operatorname{Ad}(g)(X\otimes1)=X\otimes1\}$ and $\operatorname{Ad}$ is the differential of conjugation. The superscript means the identity component with its open-subscheme structure. Each $K_X$ is a smooth geometrically connected closed subgroup with $\dim K_X<\dim G$ [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension], its tangent space inside $\mathfrak g$ is $\{Y:[Y,X]=0\}$, and these subspaces span $\mathfrak g$ over $k$. In particular the indexing set of rational noncentral semisimple $X$ is nonempty. No perfectness or characteristic hypothesis is imposed.

source.place: Propositions 17.76–17.79, printed pp.377–378, and the first infinite-field case in Theorem 17.91, p.381. The identity component has the same tangent space; properness and dimension drop use 17.77 and 10.15. Over an imperfect field use restricted powers to obtain rational semisimple elements, rather than rational Jordan parts.

proof.text: Fix any rational noncentral semisimple $X$. Apply [lem-sfb-semisimple-tangent-stabilizer] to the given closed representation of $G$. Geometric connectedness implies connectedness by taking the extension $k/k$; the representation has positive dimension since a closed subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}_0=1$ cannot have a geometric noncentral tangent vector. The lemma therefore gives a smooth closed finite-type affine subgroup $C=C_G(X)$ and identifies its tangent image with $\{Y:[Y,X]=0\}$. Noncentrality makes this a proper subspace of $\mathfrak g$: choose $Y$ with $[X,Y]\ne0$ and use antisymmetry. Consequently $C\ne G$, since equality would give equality of tangent images.

source.place: Propositions 17.76 and 17.77, printed p.377; faithful-matrix formulation as in the cited stabilizer node.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-finite-type-group-identity-subgroup] to $C$. Its identity component $K_X$ is a connected open and closed subgroup with the specified open-subscheme structure. As a closed subscheme of the affine finite-type scheme $C$, it is affine of finite type (its coordinate algebra is a quotient of $k[C]$). The successive quotient maps also show that its inclusion in $G$ is closed. The open inclusion into the smooth $C$ is smooth over $k$ by [lem-pc-open-immersion-smooth-composition] (Stacks Tags 01VC and 01VA). The identity is a $k$-point of $K_X$, so [lem-sbc-connected-rational-point-geometrically-connected] (Tag 04KV) makes $K_X$ geometrically connected. All three cited assertions allow arbitrary base fields.

source.place: Proposition 1.34, printed pp.16–17; Proposition 17.76, p.377. Stacks Tags 0B7R, 01VC, 01VA and 04KV for identity subgroup, smooth restriction and geometric connectedness.

proof.text: The tangent spaces of $C$ and its open identity component agree inside $\mathfrak g$. Indeed a tangent vector is a map $\operatorname{Spec}(k[\epsilon]/\epsilon^2)\to C$ reducing to the identity, by [lem-sfb-affine-group-dual-number-calculus]. The source has just one underlying point, which maps to the identity in $K_X$. The open-factorization assertion [lem-weil-pbc-morphism-factors-through-open-subscheme] (Tag 01HI) gives a unique factorization through $K_X$. Conversely compose a tangent vector of $K_X$ with its inclusion. These operations are inverse and respect the tangent inclusions by naturality in the dual-number calculus. Thus $\operatorname{Lie}(K_X)=\operatorname{Lie}(C)=\{Y:[Y,X]=0\}$.

source.place: Proposition 1.34 and Sections 10.6, 10.14, printed pp.16–17, 188–190; open restriction of tangent vectors, Stacks Tag 01HI.

proof.text: For $J=K_X,G$, [lem-ag-smooth-lie-local-dimension] gives $\dim_k\operatorname{Lie}(J)=\dim\mathcal O_{J,e}$ and [lem-ag-group-identity-local-dimension] gives $\dim\mathcal O_{J,e}=\dim J$. Here these are the same tangent Lie spaces as above; both dimension statements apply over $k$, not merely over an algebraic closure. The tangent subspace of $K_X$ is proper by steps 1 and 3. Extend a basis of it by a vector outside it and then to a basis of $\mathfrak g$. It follows that $\dim K_X<\dim G$. This proves every asserted geometric property for each index $X$, independently of the existence and spanning argument that follows.

source.place: The dimension calculation underlying Proposition 10.15, printed pp.190–191, and Proposition 17.77, p.377.

proof.text: Let $d=\dim_k\mathfrak g$, finite by [lem-sfb-affine-group-dual-number-calculus], and choose a basis. By [lem-sfb-affine-group-lie-tangent-calculus], identify $\mathfrak g$ with its faithful tangent matrix image, the bracket with matrix commutator, and $\operatorname{Lie}(G_{\bar k})$ with $\bar k\otimes_k\mathfrak g$. The adjoint representation $\operatorname{Ad}=\operatorname{Ad}_G:G\to\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak g)\cong\operatorname{GL}_{d,k}$ of [lem-sfb-affine-group-dual-number-calculus] has differential $\operatorname{ad}$: its conjugation formula for $\operatorname{GL}_{n,k}$, with $E(B)=I+\delta B$, gives $\operatorname{Ad}(h)B=hBh^{-1}$, and naturality for $i$ gives $di(\operatorname{Ad}(g)Z)=i(g)\,di(Z)\,i(g)^{-1}$. For $g=t_Y$, $i(t_Y)=I+\epsilon\,di(Y)$ and $(I+\epsilon A)B(I-\epsilon A)=B+\epsilon(AB-BA)$; injectivity and bracket compatibility of $di$ give $d\operatorname{Ad}(Y)=\operatorname{ad}(Y)$. Write $\det(T-\operatorname{ad}(Y))=T^d+f_1(Y)T^{d-1}+\cdots+f_d(Y)$. The entries of $\operatorname{ad}(Y)$ are linear in $Y$, so the determinant formula makes each $f_i$ a polynomial over $k$. Choose the geometric noncentral semisimple element $S$ in the hypothesis and diagonalize its faithful tangent matrix over $\bar k$. On all matrices, commutation with that diagonal matrix is diagonal in the matrix-unit basis. Its invariant subspace $\mathfrak g_{\bar k}$ is a sum of eigenspaces: polynomial spectral projections recover each component. Thus $\operatorname{ad}(S)$ is diagonalizable and nonzero, so it has a nonzero eigenvalue. Its characteristic polynomial is not $T^d$. Fix $f=f_i$ with $f_i(S)\ne0$; in particular $f$ is a nonzero polynomial over $k$.

source.place: Proposition 17.78 and the first sentence of 17.79, printed p.378; matrix spectral-projection calculation expands the adjoint criterion.

proof.text: For every $Y\in\mathfrak g(k)$ with $f(Y)\ne0$, $\operatorname{ad}(Y)$ has a nonzero eigenvalue over $\bar k$. Suppose first that $\operatorname{char}k=0$. This field is perfect: the derivative of a nonconstant irreducible polynomial is nonzero of smaller degree, hence coprime to that polynomial, so the polynomial has no repeated geometric roots. Apply [lem-sfb-algebraic-lie-additive-jordan] over $k$ and put $X=Y_s$. Its faithful matrix is diagonalizable; the commuting decomposition gives $[Y,X]=0$. Applied to the rational adjoint representation, whose differential is $\operatorname{ad}$ by step 5, the same lemma identifies $\operatorname{ad}(X)$ with the semisimple part of $\operatorname{ad}(Y)$. In a basis diagonalizing the semisimple part, its commuting nilpotent part restricts to each eigenspace and has only zero eigenvalues there. Hence the eigenvalues of $\operatorname{ad}(Y)$ are those of its semisimple part. The nonzero eigenvalue persists, so $\operatorname{ad}(X)\ne0$. Thus $X$ is rational noncentral semisimple and $Y$ lies in its bracket centralizer.

source.place: Propositions 17.74 and 17.79, printed pp.377–378; the characteristic-zero rational Jordan-part argument.

proof.text: If $\operatorname{char}k=p>0$, apply [lem-sfb-restricted-rational-differentiation] to $G$, its faithful representation and its adjoint representation. Its tangent vectors are the point derivations $x$ with $t_x(a)=\varepsilon(a)+x(a)\epsilon$ on $k[G]$; for a representation $r$ with matrix coefficients $c_{ab}$ the operator $\rho(x)$ has entries $x(c_{ab})$, which by $r(t_x)=I+\epsilon\,dr(x)$ [lem-sfb-affine-group-lie-tangent-calculus] are those of $dr(x)$. So $\rho=di$ for $i$ and $\rho=d\operatorname{Ad}=\operatorname{ad}$ (step 5) for the adjoint comodule. For $q=p^N$, the rational vector $X=Y^{[p^N]}$ has faithful matrix $M^q$, where $M=di(Y)$, and $\operatorname{ad}(X)=\operatorname{ad}(Y)^q$. Over the perfect field $\bar k$, [lem-sfb-algebraic-lie-additive-jordan] writes $M=M_s+M_n$ with commuting diagonalizable and nilpotent parts. Choose $N$ so that $q$ is at least a nilpotence exponent of $M_n$. The commuting binomial formula in characteristic $p$ gives $M^q=M_s^q$, which is diagonalizable. The nonzero eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $\operatorname{ad}(Y)$ gives the nonzero eigenvalue $\lambda^q$ of $\operatorname{ad}(X)$, so $X$ is noncentral. Finally $M$ commutes with $M^q$; injectivity and bracket compatibility of the tangent matrix map from step 5 give $[Y,X]=0$. Thus the same conclusion as step 6 holds over every imperfect field as well, without taking rational Jordan parts.

source.place: Proposition 17.79, printed p.378, with the restricted-power construction preceding 11.36, p.223; agent expansion of the imperfect-field descent omitted in the printed proof.

proof.text:
Let $W\subseteq\mathfrak g$ be the $k$-linear span of all bracket centralizers of rational noncentral semisimple elements. Steps 6–7 show that $W$ contains every rational $Y$ with $f(Y)
e0$. A nonzero polynomial over an infinite field has a rational nonzero value: induct on the number of variables, choose the first variables to keep a nonzero coefficient in the last variable nonzero, then avoid the finitely many roots in the last variable; for zero variables the assertion is immediate. Applying this to $f$ produces such a $Y$, so steps 6–7 also prove that the indexing set is nonempty. If $W$ were proper, extend a basis to construct a nonzero linear form $\ell$ vanishing on $W$. The polynomial $f\ell$ is nonzero: multiply leading monomials in a monomial order, whose coefficients have nonzero product in the field. Apply the same polynomial argument to obtain a rational $Y$ with $f(Y)\ell(Y)
e0$. Then $Y\in W$ but $\ell(Y)
e0$, a contradiction. Hence $W=\mathfrak g$. Step 3 identifies its constituent subspaces with the tangent spaces of the asserted $K_X$, completing the spanning assertion.

lean.note: The helper declarations belong to the notions explicitly introduced by this statement. Scalar extension abbreviates the existing pullback functor on group objects; geometricTangentMatrix computes the actual base-changed differential on dual-number points. Centralizer specifies the given adjoint stabilizer functor by its faithful matrix equations on every commutative test algebra; the theorem asserts existence without choosing any object from a sorry. Identity components and tangent differentials are the existing upstream constructions.
